results.evidence: No statute numbers or section references appear anywhere in the post; legal rules described using general language like 'most jurisdictions require regular calibration' and 'officers need reasonable suspicion'
No individual attorney or legal-scholar names appear; only NHTSA (a federal agency) is referenced as a source

The one statistic — 'misidentify sober people as impaired 18% of the time' — is sourced to 'NHTSA HS 178 R2/06' in the same sentence; all other numbers (.08, .06, $7,000, 47 days) are hypothetical examples, not factual claims

Procedural claims are jurisdiction-qualified: 'Most jurisdictions require regular calibration on manufacturer-specified intervals' and 'In most states, a required 15-minute observation period'; no bare universal deadlines or filing requirements
No case citations appear; 'fruit of the poisonous tree' is a legal doctrine reference, not a case citation
Consequence language is narrative and general — 'your freedom, your license, and your record' — with no specific collateral-consequence claims stated as universal fact

results.reason: No question_count field in frontmatter; title promises 5 questions and body delivers 5 numbered attorney questions plus follow-ups, consistent with headline.

Multiple unsourced factual claims: 'most attorneys never request calibration records,' 'breathalyzer machines drift over time,' '15-minute observation period' in most states, and 'calibrated 47 days late' example lack inline sources beyond the single NHTSA HS 178 R2/06 citation.
Action items use plain language ('Ask your attorney today,' 'Email your attorney today') and legal terms like motion to suppress are immediately defined in-line.
None of the banned cliches ('end of the day,' 'tip of the iceberg,' 'slippery slope,' 'double-edged sword,' 'game changer,' 'wake-up call') appear in the post.
Post maintains second-person 'you/your' throughout with no drift to 'the defendant' or third person for consecutive sentences.
Passive constructions ('was calibrated,' 'were administered') appear but remain well under 30% of sentences; most sentences are active voice.
Legal terms like motion to suppress, motion to compel discovery, motion in limine, and fruit of the poisonous tree are each defined on first use within bullet explanations or inline context.
Logical flow: scenario hook -> 5 numbered questions each following problem/context/action pattern -> 'Why These Questions Matter' synthesis -> CTAs.
Multiple clear CTAs present: Case Progress Score link, DUI Defense Playbook link, and specific attorney questions with exact scripts to use today.
Action statements are direct imperatives ('Ask your attorney today,' 'Call your attorney's office right now,' 'Email your attorney today') with hedging reserved for informational claims.
No paragraph exceeds 300 words; action-oriented paragraphs stay concise, typically 2-4 sentences each.
The five numbered question sections are roughly proportional in length with no single section approaching 50% of total word count.
Threats (license/job/record loss, DUI charge, 'controls your life') are consistently followed within 1-2 sentences by specific actions like calling the attorney or requesting calibration records.
Strong opening scenario hook ('You got pulled over. You blew a number.'), middle builds with evidence and specific attorney behaviors, closing empowers with exact scripts and product CTAs.

results.evidence: Post contains direct directives like 'Call your attorney's office right now and ask one question', 'Email your attorney today with this exact sentence', and 'Write down the date they give you' — commands the reader should follow.
Each section directs the reader back to their attorney with specific questions to ask, keeping attorney consultation proximate throughout.
Post discusses legal concepts generally without evaluating the reader's specific case strength or likelihood of conviction.

Post recommends specific motions the attorney should file: 'Motion to suppress. Motion to dismiss. Motion to compel discovery' and 'your attorney should be filing a motion to address it' regarding missing footage.
Post does not discuss immigration consequences, so the immigration redirect requirement does not apply.
Post does not mention collateral consequences like professional licenses, housing, firearms, or voting rights.
Post references only general categories like 'your attorney' and 'a flat-fee attorney' without naming specific firms or companies.
Post does not use 'we recommend' phrasing; explicitly states 'We're not telling you what to do. We're giving you the questions to ask.'

Hypothetical strategy example ('I've reviewed the dashcam footage and the stop appears pretextual — the officer cited a broken taillight...') is not labeled as hypothetical and could be mistaken for a real case.

Post explicitly frames content as questions to ask the attorney, stating 'These five questions aren't designed to be adversarial. They're designed to tell you whether your attorney is actually working your case.'

Post makes absolute claims like 'If the stop was illegal, everything that follows is fruit of the poisonous tree' and 'Officers need reasonable suspicion to pull you over' without qualifiers like 'in general' or 'typically' or jurisdiction variation notes.

Post implies outcomes: 'If the stop was illegal, every piece of evidence that followed it can be thrown out' and 'A surprising number of DUI cases are won or lost on this single issue' without qualification that results vary.

Legal strategies like fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine, motion to suppress applications, and pretextual stop challenges are presented as the blog's own positions without attribution to specific cases, statutes, or named legal authorities.
No contradictory legal claims appear within the post.

Products framed as research/preparation tools: 'Case Progress Score' tells you 'what to ask next' and the Playbook gives 'everything you need to hold your attorney accountable' — not as attorney replacement.
